analysis.one_liner: Lets states win federal grants to set up their own universal health care systems.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 44 cosponsors, was referred to a House subcommittee in August 2003 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let up to ten states get federal planning grants and up to five states get demonstration grants to build their own universal, comprehensive health coverage systems with simplified administration. Participating states could pool federal money now spent on Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and federal employee coverage, and could waive the federal law (ERISA) that normally stops states from regulating employer health plans. States had to cover everyone at benefit levels at least equal to a standard Blue Cross plan and could not raise federal health spending above what it would have been otherwise.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 44 million uninsured Americans at the time, starting with residents of the up to ten states that could take part: they would gain coverage regardless of job, income, or health status, with benefits at least equal to the standard Blue Cross federal employee plan, no increase in premiums or cost-sharing for people already on federal programs, and guaranteed re-enrollment in federal programs if they moved to a non-participating state [S3]. States would also gain administrative simplicity by pooling federal health funds instead of running fragmented programs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Up to ten states could get planning grants of up to $3.75 million each, and up to five states could then win seven-year demonstration grants plus a transition grant of up to $10 million plus $3 per resident, to design and launch a universal, comprehensive health care system with simplified administration.

Participating states could pool money the federal government would otherwise pay for Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and federal employee health coverage, and could get a waiver of ERISA — the federal law that normally prevents states from regulating employer health plans — so employer and public dollars could flow into one state system.

States had to cover all residents regardless of employment, income, or preexisting conditions, with a benefits floor at least equal to the standard Blue Cross/Blue Shield federal employee plan, and could not cut benefits or raise cost-sharing for people already covered by federal programs.

Residents of a participating state who moved away were guaranteed immediate re-enrollment in Medicare, Medicaid, or other federal programs they would otherwise qualify for, so joining the state system could not leave them stranded.

Each state plan had to include public participation in planning, an analysis projecting whether the new system would cost less than the status quo over seven years, and quality-assurance mechanisms — and federal health spending in the state could not exceed what it would have been without the plan.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the planning grants, transition grants, and a 3-percentage-point increase in each state's federal Medicaid matching rate during the demonstration [S3]. Health insurers would lose premiums and market share in any state that adopted a universal public system, since employer and public dollars would be pooled into the state plan [S3]. Employers would move from paying premiums to contributing to the state system, and state budgets could not reduce their own health spending under the plan [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; health insurers in participating states

drawbacks.text: The scale was small by design: only ten states could plan and only five could implement a system, so even full success would have covered a fraction of the country and proved little about national reform.

The federal government would add new costs — transition grants of up to $10 million plus $3 per resident, and a 3-percentage-point boost to each state's Medicaid match for the life of the demonstration — on top of the federal money pooled into the state system.

Waiving ERISA and pooling Medicare and Medicaid funds would have dismantled existing employer-based coverage and known program rules in participating states, a major transition risk for the businesses and patients involved, even with the bill's audits, benefit floors, and requirement that federal spending not exceed the status quo.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design was careful for its type: a hard cap on federal spending, an independent audit to protect the Medicare trust funds, a benefits floor, and guaranteed re-entry into federal programs if a resident moved away [S3]. Its main weakness was scale — a five-state demonstration would have left national coverage gaps untouched — and the real transition risks fell on employers, insurers, and patients in whichever states tried it. The heavier cost to ordinary people came not from the bill's terms but from its death: no hearing, no debate, no vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, passed down to the Health Subcommittee a week later, and never came back out — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Tierney introduced the bill on July 25, 2003, joined by 44 original cosponsors — 43 Democrats and the Independent Bernard Sanders; no Republicans signed on.
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and on August 8, 2003 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health.
That subcommittee referral is the last recorded action; the bill never received a hearing, a committee markup, or a floor vote, and died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and the existing employer-based insurance system, which kept their premiums and their role unchallenged in every state. Uninsured residents of the states that might have taken part gained nothing, because the demonstration never got past a subcommittee referral.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and the insurance status quo

for.name: Rep. John Tierney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 44 original cosponsors.

for.name: 43 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors at introduction, including members such as Dennis Kucinich, Jim McDermott, Pete Stark, Sherrod Brown ally Sherrod Brown's colleagues Barney Frank and Maxine Waters; the list spans the party's progressive wing.

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: The only non-Democrat cosponsor; a longtime single-payer advocate who signed on at introduction.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never brought the bill to a markup or floor vote; the record shows no committee action after the bill reached the Health Subcommittee.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the House agenda and never scheduled the bill for consideration; not one House Republican cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All 45 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Bernard Sanders — no Republican signed on — and the Republican-chaired committee of referral never acted on the bill, so the fault line ran by party even though no formal vote was ever taken.

industries.note: A state universal system pooling Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, and federal employee funds — with ERISA waived — would replace private premiums with a public plan in participating states. Insurers kept that business only because the bill died in committee.

The ERISA waiver would have shifted employers from running health plans to paying into a state pool; the bill's findings argued businesses would save billions if health spending grew at the economy's rate, but participation would have upended existing benefit arrangements.

Providers would gain paying patients from universal coverage while the uninsured's unpaid bills stopped being cost-shifted onto others, but state plans had to show cost containment, which typically means payment pressure on hospitals and drug spending.
